source_scope: Diseases of Swine, 11th Edition, pages 401-600 markdown extraction
note: These are paraphrased operational facts derived from pages 401-600. They should be reviewed before insertion into exports/knowledge_facts.json.

candidate_facts.subject: swine reproductive failure
candidate_facts.object: Reproductive failure investigations should use herd records, return timing, farrowing rate, fetal stage, sow illness status, semen and insemination context, and management/toxin risk before assigning a pathogen.

candidate_facts.subject: porcine abortion
candidate_facts.object: If aborting sows are clinically ill at or near abortion, specimens from both the dam and fetuses should be submitted because maternal systemic illness and fetal infection have different diagnostic windows.

candidate_facts.subject: porcine fetal infection diagnosis
candidate_facts.object: When fetal infection is suspected, sampling multiple fetuses per litter from multiple litters reduces the risk of missing agents because not all fetuses are infected at the time of abortion.

candidate_facts.subject: porcine abortion fetal specimens
candidate_facts.object: Porcine abortion workups may require formalin-fixed and fresh/chilled brain, heart, lung, liver, spleen, kidney, placenta, skeletal muscle, fetal thoracic fluid, fetal stomach contents, and dam serum or other dam samples.

candidate_facts.subject: influenza-associated abortion
candidate_facts.object: Influenza A-associated abortion reflects maternal illness; fetuses are not acceptable specimens to identify IAV as the initiating cause, so nasal or bronchial swabs, lung, oral fluids, or paired serology from sick dams are more appropriate.

candidate_facts.subject: bacterial abortion
candidate_facts.object: Assigning bacteria as the cause of abortion requires compatible microscopic lesions such as placentitis or pneumonia plus culture evidence consistent with significant infection rather than contamination.

candidate_facts.subject: swine abortion stillbirth and mummification
candidate_facts.object: Swine abortion, stillbirth, mummification, weak-born pigs, and infertility differentials include PRRSV, PCV2, PPV, PRV, IAV, EMCV, enteroviruses/teschoviruses, CSF, ASF, atypical pestiviruses, JEV, PCMV, rubulavirus, Menangle virus, Leptospira, Brucella suis, Chlamydia, carbon monoxide, and zearalenone.

candidate_facts.subject: swine respiratory disease
candidate_facts.object: Respiratory disease often develops when mucociliary, macrophage, antibody, and cell-mediated defenses are impaired or overwhelmed by environment, stress, crowding, mixing, primary pathogens, or opportunistic bacteria.

candidate_facts.subject: porcine respiratory disease complex
candidate_facts.object: PRDC commonly involves multiple viral and bacterial agents plus environmental, management, genetic, and immune factors, so diagnosis should not assume a single pathogen from cough or pneumonia alone.

candidate_facts.subject: respiratory disease control
candidate_facts.object: Herd respiratory control should reduce pathogen load, minimize factors that damage respiratory defenses, and maximize host resistance through environment, pig flow, biosecurity, pathogen elimination, and vaccination strategy.

candidate_facts.subject: respiratory disease monitoring
candidate_facts.object: Respiratory diagnostics should have a clear objective and integrate herd history, clinical signs, necropsy, gross and microscopic lesions, lab testing, serology, nasal swabs, oral fluids, and slaughter checks as appropriate.

candidate_facts.subject: renal petechiae in pigs
candidate_facts.object: Renal petechiae can occur with bacterial septicemia, CSF, ASF, cytomegalovirus, electrocution, intoxications, acute glomerulonephritis, and other conditions, so they should not be treated as diagnostic for one disease alone.

candidate_facts.subject: swine renal failure
candidate_facts.object: Renal failure should be interpreted as prerenal, primary renal, or postrenal based on blood flow, renal parenchymal disease, obstruction, BUN/creatinine, urine findings, and gross lesions.

candidate_facts.subject: cystitis pyelonephritis in sows
candidate_facts.object: Cystitis-pyelonephritis evaluation can use frequent micturition, bloodstained or cloudy urine, urine sediment, BUN/creatinine, ocular-fluid urea after death, and gross lesions of cystitis, ureteritis, pyelitis, papillary necrosis, and suppurative renal inflammation.

candidate_facts.subject: virus detection
candidate_facts.object: Virus culture, antigen tests, nucleic-acid tests, antibody tests, sequencing, and quantitation answer different diagnostic questions and must be interpreted with disease stage, tissue tropism, sample quality, and clinical/pathologic compatibility.

candidate_facts.subject: porcine adenoviruses
candidate_facts.object: Porcine adenoviruses are widely distributed and may be found in healthy pigs, so detection should be interpreted with compatible lesions and exclusion of more likely causes before assigning causality.

candidate_facts.subject: African swine fever
candidate_facts.object: ASF in domestic pigs and European wild boar may present with high fever, depression, hemorrhagic or cyanotic skin lesions, abortion, respiratory distress from pulmonary edema, splenomegaly, hemorrhagic lymph nodes, renal petechiae, and high mortality depending on virus virulence.

candidate_facts.subject: African swine fever
candidate_facts.object: ASF clinical signs and lesions resemble CSF, erysipelas, septicemic salmonellosis, and other hemorrhagic diseases; laboratory testing is essential for definitive diagnosis.

candidate_facts.subject: African swine fever
candidate_facts.object: ASF laboratory evaluation may use lymph nodes, kidney, spleen, lung, blood, and serum; bone marrow from the leg can be useful for wild-boar testing.

candidate_facts.subject: African swine fever suspicion
candidate_facts.object: When ASF is suspected, pig movements should be restricted and diagnostic testing performed immediately; routine treatment, sale, or movement advice is inappropriate.

candidate_facts.subject: PCV2 systemic disease
candidate_facts.object: PCV2-SD diagnosis requires compatible wasting or growth retardation, moderate to severe characteristic lymphoid histopathology, and moderate to high PCV2 amount within lesions.

candidate_facts.subject: PCV2 qualitative PCR
candidate_facts.object: Qualitative PCR alone should not diagnose PCV2-SD because PCV2 is ubiquitous and positive results without compatible clinical disease and lesions are common.

candidate_facts.subject: PCV2 reproductive disease
candidate_facts.object: Late-gestation PCV2 reproductive disease diagnosis requires late-term abortion or stillbirths, fetal heart lesions such as fibrosing or necrotizing myocarditis, and high PCV2 amount in myocardial lesions and other fetal tissues.

candidate_facts.subject: porcine dermatitis and nephropathy syndrome
candidate_facts.object: PDNS diagnosis is based on hemorrhagic or necrotizing skin lesions and/or swollen pale kidneys with cortical petechiae plus systemic necrotizing vasculitis and necrotizing fibrinous glomerulonephritis.

candidate_facts.subject: PDNS gross lesions
candidate_facts.object: PDNS gross lesions involving dark skin discoloration and renal petechiae can resemble CSF and ASF, so high-risk hemorrhagic disease differentials should remain active.

candidate_facts.subject: transmissible gastroenteritis
candidate_facts.object: TGE in susceptible herds causes vomiting, profuse watery yellowish diarrhea, rapid dehydration, and high morbidity and mortality in pigs under two weeks of age, with severity inversely related to age.

candidate_facts.subject: TGEV PEDV and PDCoV enteric disease
candidate_facts.object: TGEV, PEDV, and PDCoV can produce small-intestinal villous atrophy and malabsorptive watery diarrhea, so differential testing and lesion context are required.

candidate_facts.subject: TGEV piglet protection
candidate_facts.object: Passive lactogenic immunity, especially milk IgA generated after intestinal immune stimulation in the sow, is critical for protecting suckling piglets against TGEV intestinal infection.

candidate_facts.subject: endemic TGE in young pigs
candidate_facts.object: Endemic TGE in suckling or recently weaned pigs can resemble PEDV, PDCoV, rotavirus, E. coli, or coccidiosis, so age, herd immunity, lesion pattern, and differential testing are needed.

candidate_facts.subject: pseudorabies Aujeszky disease
candidate_facts.object: PRV can cause fatal neurologic disease in young pigs, respiratory or inapparent infection in older pigs, and resorption, mummification, abortion, stillbirths, or weak-born pigs in pregnant animals.

candidate_facts.subject: pseudorabies virus
candidate_facts.object: PRV spreads through swine secretions, excretions, aerosols, contaminated fomites, breeding or semen exposure, transplacental transmission, and movement of latently infected pigs that may reactivate under stress.

candidate_facts.subject: pseudorabies diagnosis
candidate_facts.object: Preferred tissues for PRV detection include trigeminal ganglia, olfactory ganglia, and tonsils, with lung, spleen, liver, kidney, lymph nodes, pharyngeal mucosa, fetal tissues, or sacral ganglia selected according to presentation and latency context.

candidate_facts.subject: pseudorabies serology
candidate_facts.object: ELISAs targeting deleted marker antigens such as gE allow differentiation of infected from vaccinated animals in PRV control and eradication programs.

candidate_facts.subject: hepatitis E virus in swine
candidate_facts.object: HEV in swine should be handled with zoonotic and food-safety context rather than routine individual pig treatment, and interpretation should distinguish infection/exposure from clinical disease.

candidate_facts.subject: Japanese encephalitis virus in swine
candidate_facts.object: JEV belongs in abortion, stillbirth, weak-piglet, boar infertility, neurologic, vector-borne, and public-health differential contexts in endemic or exposure-compatible settings.

candidate_facts.subject: influenza A virus in swine
candidate_facts.object: Swine influenza A has a bidirectional human-swine interface; human-to-swine transmission is frequent, reassortment is common, and respiratory outbreaks should consider public-health and animal-health boundaries.
